beats.role_note: EXECUTIVE-SUMMARY LAW: the hesitant writer types the misconception (react faster) and corrects it to the film's claim (plan ahead).
beats.narration_text: New servers take minutes to boot, so an autoscaler that only reacts is already late, and requests wait. It has to plan ahead, and yesterday's traffic shows when.

beats.role_note: the environment, shown running: real AutoscaleEnv output (Kubernetes-style threshold policy, held-out app 8c2b9304 day 10, minutes 898-913)
beats.narration_text: This week I built a simulated server cluster as a Gymnasium environment. Each step is one minute. The agent adds or removes servers, pays for every server, and loses points for every late request.
beats.new_visual_element: 50 server slots, booting servers counting down, load against capacity, reward per minute

the clock ticks one minute per step; new servers appear outlined with a 3-minute countdown, then turn teal
a load bar rises past the capacity line; the overflow is counted as late requests in crimson
the reward line from env.py: reward = -(cost + late_penalty * late)

shot.visual_intent: Left: 5x10 grid of server slots. Right: requests this minute vs serving capacity (600 per server), late requests in crimson, and the reward code line. Data: evidence.json burst.* (threshold run).

beats.role_note: real traffic: 19 apps from the Azure Functions trace, 14 training and 5 held out
beats.narration_text: Then I replaced my made-up traffic with real traffic: nineteen web apps from Microsoft's public Azure Functions trace, fourteen days each. Fourteen apps train the agent. Five stay hidden for testing.
beats.new_visual_element: 19 real 14-day traces, split 14 train / 5 held out, then one app zoomed

14 sparklines tint teal (train), 5 tint slate (held out)
brackets: days 1-10 train, days 11-14 unseen

shot.visual_intent: A 4x5 grid of real hourly traces (each scaled to its own peak). Data: evidence.json grid.

beats.role_note: the burst arrives in one minute; the threshold rule's capacity lags; 72% of training bursts peak in their first minute
beats.narration_text: Seventy-two percent of bursts reach their peak in the first minute. Nothing can boot a server that fast, and the Kubernetes rule only adds servers after the load arrives. So reacting is not enough. The only defence is spare capacity.
beats.new_visual_element: a real one-minute burst with the threshold rule's capacity lagging, and the minutes-to-peak histogram

show.event: histogram of minutes from burst start to peak; the first bar grows to 72%
a 3-minute boot marker sits to its right
the real burst draws on: requests per minute jump in one minute
the Kubernetes threshold capacity steps up minutes later; the gap fills crimson (late requests)

shot.visual_intent: Left: minutes-to-peak bars (evidence.json peak_dist). Right: held-out app 8c2b9304 day 10, minutes 896-917, load vs threshold capacity (evidence.json burst).

beats.role_note: yesterday's traffic had the same burst at the same minute; the agent observes the next 10 minutes of yesterday
beats.narration_text: But many bursts come back at the same time the next day. So the agent also sees what traffic did at this time yesterday.
beats.new_visual_element: yesterday's load overlaid on today's, with the 10-minute look-ahead window

the same-time-yesterday rule's capacity rises before the burst; the crimson gap shrinks

shot.visual_intent: Same window as B04, layered. Data: evidence.json burst (yesterday, cap_yesterday, late_yesterday).

beats.role_note: results on 5 held-out apps, 65 unseen days (scripts/demo.py): cost against late requests
beats.narration_text: On five apps it had never seen, a simple same time yesterday rule cut late requests from five and a half percent to just over one percent. The Kubernetes rule stayed worse even when it spent more on servers.
beats.new_visual_element: cost (server-minutes per day) against late requests, five policies

Kubernetes threshold point lands at 5.47%
an arrow slides down to same time yesterday at 1.17%
the threshold rule at a 50% target lands at 27,371 and 3.10%, still above
linear forecast and fixed-for-the-peak points complete the picture

beats.role_note: recap card; the narration carries the takeaway
beats.narration_text: Let's recap with Claude. If your autoscaler only reacts, check whether your traffic repeats each day. Using yesterday's pattern can cut waiting requests by more than half.

show.event: the artifact card lists four lines, one per idea

artifactLines: Data: 19 real Azure web apps; 5 held out for testing.
72% of bursts peak in their first minute.
A new server needs 3 minutes, so reacting is late.
Same time yesterday: late requests 5.47% down to 1.17%.
Next: a PPO agent must beat that at equal cost.

beats.role_note: HANDOFF LAW: the prompt is read aloud verbatim, then discussed
beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude. Here are two weeks of my service's requests per minute. Find the bursts, and tell me how many come back at the same time the next day. If many do, you can plan ahead instead of reacting.

cli_exercise.ask: Here are two weeks of my service's requests per minute. Find the bursts, and tell me how many come back at the same time the next day.
cli_exercise.output_description: A list of bursts (start minute, height, length) and the share that repeat within a few minutes of the same time on another day.
cli_exercise.change: Compare that share with bursts placed at random times on the same days.
cli_exercise.output2_description: The repeat share next to the random-timing share; a large gap means yesterday's traffic is a usable signal.
cli_exercise.next_step: Run it on your own service's per-minute request log.
